articles.text: TĀNGMǓ: Nǐ zài kàn shénme bàozhǐ?
TOM: What newspaper are you reading?
LǏ PÍNG: Míng Bào. Míng Bào bú cuò, hěn yǒu yìsi.
LǏ PÍNG: Ming Pao. It's pretty good, very interesting.
LǏ WÉN: Zài Měiguo yě xiàng Xiānggǎng zhèiyàng, shénme luànqībāzāode xīnwén dōu wǎng bàozhǐshang xiě ma?
LǏ WÉN: In America is it the same as in Hong Kong: they put all kinds of crazy news in the paper?

TĀNGMǓ: Píngcháng wǒ kàn Huáshèngdùn Yóubào. Zhèige bàozhǐ bú cuò, guónèi, guówàide xīnwén dōu yǒu, dāngrán guǎnggào yě bù shǎo. Zhōngwén bàozhǐ, wǒ yě kàn, nèi shàngbianr yě yǒu nǐ shuōde nèizhǒng "luànqībāzāo" de xīnwén.

TOM: I usually read the Washington Post. It's a pretty good paper. It has domestic as well as international news. Of course there are a lot of ads, too. I read Chinese newspapers too, and they have "all kinds of crazy news" in them, as you put it.
LǏ PÍNG: Nǐmen zhèiyàng shuō, wǒ bù zěnme tóngyì. Shénme shi "luànqībāzāo"? Shèhuì shēnghuó běnlái jiù shi zhèiyàng ma!
LǏ PÍNG: I don't really agree with what you are saying. What is "all kinds of crazy news"? That's exactly the way life in society is!
LǏ WÉN: Suàn le ba! Jīntian shi shā rén, míngtian shi xī dú, wǒ bú yào kàn.
LǏ WÉN: Forget it! Today it's killing, tomorrow it's drugs. I don't want to read that.
TĀNGMǓ: Kàn háishi xūyào kànde, yīnwei shèhuì shēnghuózhōngde wèntí, wǒmen yě bù néng bù zhùyì a!
TOM: We still need to read it, because we can't very well ignore the problems of life in society.
LǏ WÉN: Xiānggǎngde shèhuì wèntí zhēn duō! Shénme dìfangrde rén dōu yǒu, shénmeyàngrde wèntí yě dōu yǒu.
LǏ WÉN: Hong Kong sure has a lot of social problems. There are people from everywhere, and all kinds of problems.
TĀNGMǓ: Shèhuì wèntí shi shìjièxìngde, bù zhǐ shi Xiānggǎng yǒu.
TOM: Problems in society are worldwide. Hong Kong isn't the only place that has them.
LǏ WÉN: Ng, nàme, rénmen duì zhèixiē wèntí jiù méiyou shénme bànfǎr ma?
LǏ WÉN: Mm, then is there nothing people can do about these problems?
LǏ PÍNG: Bànfǎ hěn duō, dìfang bù tóng, bànfǎ yě bù yíyàng. Kěshi zhèixiē bànfǎ shi bu shi yǒu xiào jiù bù zhīdào le.
LǏ PÍNG: There are a lot of ways to deal with them. Different places have different ways of dealing with them. But whether these ways work or not is another question.
TĀNGMǓ: Yǒu rén shuō zōngjiào shi yìzhǒng bànfǎ, bù guǎn shénme jiào, dōu shi jiào rén zuò hǎo shìrde. Kěshi wǒ xiǎng jiàoyu hěn zhòngyào, shòu jiàoyude rén yuè duō, shèhuìde wèntí yuè shǎo.

TOM: Some people say that religion is one way. No matter what the religion, it always teaches people to do good. But I think education is important. The more educated people there are, the fewer social problems there will be.
LǏ PÍNG: Érqiě jīngjì fādá yě hěn yàojǐn. Jīngjì bù fādáde dìfang, rénmen fàn zuìde jīhui jiù gèng duō.
LǏ PÍNG: And also, a developed economy is important. In places where the economy isn't well-developed, there are more opportunities for people to commit crimes.
LǏ WÉN: Jiù shi ma, rén yào chī fàn, lián fàn dōu chībubǎo, tāmen zěnme néng bú fàn zuì ne?
LǏ WÉN: Exactly. People have to eat. If they can't even get enough to eat, how can you expect them not to commit crimes?
TĀNGMǓ: Wǒ xiǎng méi nàme jiǎndān. Fàn zuì hé hěn duō shì yǒu guānxi, tèbié shi hé jiātíng yǒu guānxi.
TOM: I don't think it's so simple. Crime is related to many different things, especially to the family.
LǏ WÉN: Nǐ jiǎngjiang kàn.
LǏ WÉN: Would you explain what you mean?

TĀNGMǓ: Zài jīngjì fādáde dìfang, xiǎo jiātíng yuè lái yuè duō, érqiě fùmǔmen dōu yǒu gōngzuò, dōu hěn máng, méiyou shíjiān duō guǎn háizi. Yǒu xiē niánqīngde fùmǔ yě hěn shǎo xiǎngdào zìjǐde zérèn, méiyou shénme jiātíng guānniàn.

TOM: Where the economy is developed, there are more and more small families; also, both parents have jobs and are very busy, so they don't have time to take good care of the children. Some young parents seldom think of their own responsibilities and don't have much of a sense of family attachment.
LǏ WÉN: Nǐde huà yǒu dàolǐ, kěshi dàlùde qíngxing ne? Nǐmen zěnme xiǎng?
LǏ WÉN: That makes sense. But what about the situation on the mainland? What do you two think?
LǏ PÍNG: Shì a. Dàlù jīngjì bù fādá, érqiě dàjiā yě dōu yǒu jiātíng guānniàn. Kěshi, kànkan bàozhǐ, dàlùshang fàn zuìde rén yě bù shǎo.

LǏ PÍNG: Yeah, the mainland's economy isn't developed, and furthermore everyone has a sense of attachment to the family. But read the papers: there are quite a few people committing crimes on the mainland too.
TĀNGMǓ: Wǒ xiǎng zhè hé zhèngzhì bù āndìng yǒu guānxi, tèbié shi cóng Liù Liù nián dào Qī Liù nián.
TOM: I think this has to do with the political instability, especially from '66 to '76.
LǏ PÍNG: Shì ma, nèige shíhou, shénme fǎlǜ dōu méiyou. Lián fàn zuì bú fàn zuì dōu nòngbuqīngchu, shèhuì wèntí zěnme huì shǎo?
LǏ PÍNG: Yes. During that time there wasn't any law at all. If you can't even tell the difference between committing a crime and not committing one, how can social problems be reduced?
TĀNGMǓ: Nǐde kànfǎ, wǒ hěn tóngyì. Wǒ xiǎng, zhǐ yǒu shǐ zhèngzhì āndìng, jīngjì, wénhuà fādá, cái néng shǐ shèhuì jìnbù.
TOM: I agree very much with your view. I think that society can only be made to progress if the political situation is stabilized and the economy and culture are made to flourish.
NǍINAI: Nǐmen zài tán shénme, tánde zhème gāoxìng?
GRANDMOTHER: What are you talking about so cheerfully?
TĀNGMǓ: Lǐ Nǎinai, wǒmen zài tán shèhuì wèntí.
TOM: We're talking about social problems, Grandma Lǐ.
NǍINAI: Hǎo le, nǐmen tángòu le meiyou? Chīle fàn zài tán xíng bu xíng?
GRANDMOTHER: Well, have you talked enough? How about continuing the conversation after dinner?
TĀNGMǓ, LǏ PÍNG, LǏ WÉN: Xíng, chīle fàn zài tán.
TOM, LǏ PÍNG AND LǏ WÉN: Okay! We'll talk more after dinner.
